newsitem.title: GERMANY: Germany's Lafontaine demands tax meeting with Kohl.
newsitem.headline: Germany's Lafontaine demands tax meeting with Kohl.

text.p: Oskar Lafontaine, leader of Germany's opposition Social Democrats (SPD), on Friday again demanded a personal meeting with Chancellor Helmut Kohl to discuss tax reforms.

Kohl has already turned down Lafontaine's call for a face-to-face meeting to restart stalled talks on the coalition government's plans to slash 30 billion marks in corporate and income taxes over two years.
But Lafontaine said he was only prepared to take part in top-level talks. He said the government's tax policies were unacceptable.
"We can't offer our help to policies which make the rich even richer and the poor poorer," Lafontaine told a conference of the east German SPD.
Lafontaine blamed Kohl for financing German unification by forcing up the costs of employing labour instead of through taxation, with negative economic consequences.

He said that labour overheads -- made up of occupational insurance costs -- had risen to 42 percent of wages from 34 percent before. High labour costs are blamed by many as the main causes of record post-war unemployment in Germany.
"Cutting these costs is the most important task we face in Germany today," Lafontaine said.
Earlier, Finance Minister Theo Waigel introduced his 1998 tax bill into parliament, the first phase of its two-year plan to cut taxes.
Talks between the coalition and SPD broke down during a recent row over coal subsidies and the party has set conditions for a resumption of the negotiations.

SPD parliamentary leader Rudolf Scharping said that the government must agree to cut labour overheads this summer, ease taxes for ordinary workers next year and put together solid counter-financing if the talks are to resume.
Failure to reach a compromise will condemn tax reforms to lengthy wrangling in parliament, where the SPD can block tax changes through its majority in the upper house.
